# Skull fractures

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General trauma > Skull fractures*

[Original Article Link](/library/8j0OXT)

---

## Summary

<u>Skull</u> <u>fractures</u> most typically occur as a result of <u>blunt force trauma</u> from contact sports, <u>motor vehicle collisions</u>, or falls. They are classified by anatomical location as either <u>cranial vault fractures</u> or <u>basilar skull fractures</u>. <u>Cranial vault fractures</u> involve one or more of the <u>cranial vault</u> bones, may be either <u>open fractures</u> or <u>closed fractures</u>, and are classified as <u>linear skull fractures</u> or <u>depressed skull fractures</u>. <u>Basilar skull fractures</u> involve one or more of the <u>skull base</u> bones and are classified as <u>anterior</u>, middle, or <u>posterior cranial fossa</u> <u>fractures</u>. Clinical features vary depending on bone involvement but may include <u>lacerations</u>, <u>contusions</u>, and <u>hematoma</u> of the scalp; palpable deformities; mobile bone fragments; <u>liquorrhea</u>; <u>Battle sign</u>; <u>raccoon eyes</u>; and <u>signs of traumatic brain injury</u>. <u>Initial management of skull fractures</u> focuses on identifying and addressing life-threatening injuries. Complications of <u>skull</u> <u>fractures</u> include <u>CSF leaks</u> (which increase the risk for <u>meningitis</u>), <u>cranial nerve disorders</u> (due to compression or transection), and <u>epidural hematomas</u>. <u>Expectant management</u> may be sufficient for simple <u>fractures</u> but neurosurgery may be necessary for <u>unstable fractures</u> and <u>fractures</u> with associated complications. <u>Open head injuries</u> can occur when <u>skull</u> <u>fractures</u> are associated with rupture of the <u>dura mater</u>, which can increase the risk of <u>CNS</u> infection.




See also “<u>Facial fractures</u>,” and “<u>Orbital floor fractures</u>” in “<u>Traumatic eye injuries</u>.”

---

## Management

### Initial management [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Follow the <u>ATLS algorithm</u> for any patient with a potentially significant <u>head injury</u>, and maintain a low threshold for early specialist consultation (e.g., neurosurgery).




* <u>Primary survey</u>

* <u>C-spine immobilization</u> and <u>neuroprotective measures</u>.

* <u>Airway management</u> and <u>mechanical ventilation</u> as needed, e.g., due to low <u>GCS</u>.

* <u>Hemostatic control</u> of obvious sources of bleeding, e.g., <u>scalp laceration management</u>.

* Perform a rapid <u>neurological examination</u>.

* If <u>signs of TBI</u> are present, begin <u>TBI management</u>.

* <u>Secondary survey</u> (once the patient is stabilized)

* Assess for <u>cranial vault</u> deformities and evidence of <u>basilar skull fractures</u>.

* Evaluate for associated injuries, e.g., <u>facial fractures</u>, <u>cervical spine injury</u>, <u>traumatic eye injuries</u>, <u>carotid or vertebral artery dissection</u>

* Obtain CT head without contrast.

* Perform further diagnostics as needed (e.g., <u>ocular examination</u>, <u>otoscopy</u>, CT <u>cervical spine</u>).





> [!WARNING]
> Assume patients with high-impact <u>head trauma</u> have a <u>cervical spine injury</u> until it has been ruled out.




> [!NOTE]
> Neurological impairment, repeated <u>vomiting</u>, and <u>seizures</u> indicate potentially severe cerebral trauma or <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u>.




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Perform <u>acute wound management</u>, including <u>scalp laceration management</u> as needed.

* Provide <u>analgesia</u> as needed.

* Consider <u>CNS infection prophylaxis for open head injury</u>.

* Consider <u>seizure prophylaxis after TBI</u>.

* See also “<u>Prevention of complications in head injuries</u>”





### Definitive management [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




See also “<u>Management of moderate and severe TBI</u>.”




* <u>Conservative management</u>: usually appropriate for nondisplaced <u>linear skull fractures</u> without significant intracranial injury

* Surgical management: may be required for comminuted or <u>depressed skull fractures</u> and/or treatment of neurovascular complications





> [!TIP]
> Determine appropriate patient disposition based on the type of <u>fracture</u> and the presence of <u>TBI</u> or other complications.

## Cranial vault fracture

### Definitions [[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)[[3]](/library/Et182i0)




* Cranial vault fracture: a <u>fracture</u> of ≥ 1 of the <u>cranial vault bones</u>; can be a closed or <u>open skull fracture</u>.

* Diastatic skull fracture: a <u>fracture</u> along the <u>skull suture lines</u> (most commonly seen in <u>newborns</u> and <u>infants</u>)





![Bones of the skull (lateral view)](media/pu7l09mxclf5qppmp5zoxodt.jpg)

Bones of the skull (lateral view)

![Cranial bones (posterior view)](media/q53nr957f6qy0ne8oafczwjx.jpg)

Cranial bones (posterior view)

![Calvaria (cranial view)](media/u4c05bh315jxwty8tsl392p5.jpg)

Calvaria (cranial view)




### Etiology




See “<u>Etiology of TBI</u>.”




### Clinical features  [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




Most commonly involves the frontal and <u>parietal bones</u>




* Scalp <u>hematoma</u>, local swelling, and tenderness

* A palpable gap along the surface of the bone or bone <u>crepitus</u> when the <u>fracture</u> fragments are moved

* <u>Scalp lacerations</u>

* <u>Epidural hematoma</u> (if in close proximity to the <u>middle meningeal artery</u>)

* <u>Signs and symptoms of TBI</u>: common in <u>depressed skull fractures</u>

* <u>Clinical features of mild TBI</u>: common in simple <u>linear skull fractures</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Use caution when examining <u>head injuries</u> to avoid pushing potential <u>depressed skull fractures</u> further into the <u>cranium</u>. [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




### Diagnostics [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/CNbqW8)




See also “<u>Diagnostics in TBI</u>.”




* CT head without IV contrast (preferred modality)  

* Evaluate for <u>fracture</u> lines.

* Assess for intracranial injury.

* <u>X-ray</u> <u>skull</u>: may be used if CT is not available





![Coup-contrecoup injury](media/aw6jy5mar28udswyxmhxoerk.jpg)

Coup-contrecoup injury

![Cranial vault fracture with epidural hematoma](media/xn7o2qv2r15vppl4m5hjzy1z.jpg)

Cranial vault fracture with epidural hematoma

![Cranial vault fracture](media/siywnxw3z9f04y9s83quw0ss.jpg)

Cranial vault fracture




### Linear skull fracture [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)




* Definition: a single <u>fracture</u> that extends through the entire width of one or more bones of the <u>skull</u>; most common type of <u>skull</u> <u>fracture</u>

* Etiology: typically occurs as a result of low-energy <u>blunt trauma</u> over a wide area of the <u>skull</u> (e.g., from a fall)

* Clinical features

* Number of <u>fracture</u> lines: simple or <u>comminuted fracture</u>

* <u>Soft tissue</u> involvement: <u>closed fracture</u> or <u>open fracture</u>

* <u>Fractures</u> crossing the middle meningeal groove or <u>dural venous sinuses</u> may result in <u>epidural hemorrhage</u>.

* Treatment

* All patients: Initiate <u>immediate management of skull fractures</u>.

* <u>Comminuted fracture</u> and/or intracranial injury: Consult neurosurgery.

* Simple linear <u>fracture</u> and no evidence of intracranial injury: <u>conservative management</u>

* Observe for 4–6 hours prior to considering discharge.  [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Return precautions</u> for any <u>red flags</u> for <u>mild TBI</u>

* See also “Management of <u>mTBI</u>.”





### Depressed skull fracture [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)




* Definition: a <u>skull</u> <u>fracture</u> in which the <u>skull</u> depresses inward toward the <u>brain</u> <u>parenchyma</u>

* Etiology: typically occurs as a result of high-energy <u>blunt trauma</u> to a small area of the <u>skull</u> (e.g., from being struck with a baseball bat)

* Clinical features

* Number of <u>fracture</u> lines: typically a <u>comminuted fracture</u>

* Often an <u>open skull fracture</u>

* Often penetrates the <u>dura</u> (i.e., causing <u>open head injury</u>) [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[3]](/library/Et182i0)

* Location: most commonly involves the parietal and frontoparietal regions

* Treatment

* Initiate <u>immediate management of skull fractures</u>.

* <u>Open depressed skull fracture</u>: See “<u>Open head injuries</u>.”

* <u>Conservative management</u>: may be appropriate for uncomplicated closed <u>depressed skull fractures</u>

* Surgical management: often required for severe or open <u>depressed skull fractures</u> and/or associated intracranial injuries

* Dispostion

* Consult neurosurgery. [[3]](/library/Et182i0)

* Admit all patients for observation.





> [!TIP]
> Open <u>depressed skull fractures</u> are often considered <u>open head injuries</u> because of the high <u>prevalence</u> of associated dural tears. <u>Antibiotic prophylaxis</u> is recommended. [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[3]](/library/Et182i0)

## Basilar skull fractures

### Definition [[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)



* A <u>skull</u> <u>fracture</u> involving ≥ 1 bone of the <u>skull base</u>, i.e., the <u>ethmoid</u>, <u>sphenoid</u>, occipital, paired frontal, and/or paired <u>temporal bones</u>




![Base of the skull (superior view of internal surface)](media/yskfijlalc32kn0wkc7l5lgu.jpg)

Base of the skull (superior view of internal surface)

![Base of the skull (inferior view of external surface)](media/w3h4vbgzl60qhizcrs70nkzq.jpg)

Base of the skull (inferior view of external surface)

![image](media/p9nzzfd2tobzlgbb2aozrrnb.jpg)



![Base of the skull: interactive 3D tour](media/ki85dl8biac6vabk037x842y.jpg)

Base of the skull: interactive 3D tour




### Etiology




See also “<u>Etiology of TBI</u>.”




* Caused by significant high-energy trauma to the <u>skull</u>

* Most commonly results from motor vehicle, motorcycle, or pedestrian-<u>motor vehicle collisions</u>

* Other causes

* Violent altercations

* Falls

* Firearms





### Classification [[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)




* <u>Anterior cranial fossa</u> <u>fracture</u>

* <u>Middle cranial fossa</u> <u>fracture</u>

* <u>Posterior cranial fossa</u> <u>fracture</u>





### Clinical features of basilar skull fractures [[5]](/library/KnbU88)[[6]](/library/dH1o6R0)




* <u>Liquorrhea</u>; : <u>CSF rhinorrhea</u> and/or <u>CSF otorrhea</u> may occur immediately or within a few days of injury

* Subcutaneous <u>hematomas</u>: typically appear within hours to days of injury

* Raccoon eyes: subcutaneous <u>hematoma</u> around the eyes

* Battle sign: subcutaneous <u>hematoma</u> overlying the <u>mastoid process</u> [[7]](/library/0-0eDi)

* <u>Cranial nerve palsies</u>

* <u>Orbit</u> and/or paranasal sinus injuries  [[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)

* <u>Hearing loss</u>, <u>vertigo</u>

* Hemotympanum: a collection of blood in the <u>tympanic cavity</u> behind the <u>tympanic membrane</u>

* Intracranial vascular injury

* <u>Internal carotid artery</u> injury  [[6]](/library/dH1o6R0)

* <u>Venous sinus thrombosis</u> or hemorrhage  [[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)[[6]](/library/dH1o6R0)

* <u>Signs and symptoms of traumatic brain injury</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>CSF otorrhea</u>, <u>hemotympanum</u>, <u>vertigo</u>, <u>hearing loss</u>, and/or <u>facial nerve palsy</u> suggest <u>fracture</u> of the petrous portion of the <u>temporal bone</u>. [[2]](/library/8G1Oai0)[[5]](/library/KnbU88)




> [!NOTE]
> <u>Raccoon eyes</u>, <u>Battle sign</u>, and <u>CSF</u> leakage are highly indicative of <u>basilar skull fractures</u>.




![Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis](media/g1634bfs0kfe9v0mw5p6giyz.jpg)

Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis

![Hemotympanum](media/qvhad3vdvrd94hyykbgd0a4u.jpg)

Hemotympanum




### Diagnostics [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/CNbqW8)[[6]](/library/dH1o6R0)




See also “<u>Diagnostics in TBI</u>.”




* CT head without IV contrast (preferred modality)  
* Findings

* Discontinuity in the bone structure with or without displacement

* <u>Pneumocephalus</u>: air within the <u>cranium</u>; typically associated with <u>open head injuries</u>

* <u>Intracranial hemorrhage</u> or <u>hematoma</u>

* <u>Hyperdensity</u> in neighboring structures (e.g., paranasal sinus, <u>middle ear</u>, <u>mastoid air cells</u>): indicates hemorrhage

* <u>CSF detection studies</u>: to evaluate for <u>cerebrospinal fluid</u> (<u>CSF</u>) in nasal and/or <u>ear discharge</u>

* Additional testing: Consider based on initial findings and clinical presentation.

* CT <u>cervical spine</u>: to rule out concomitant <u>cervical spine injury</u>

* CT maxillofacial and/or <u>temporal bone</u> without IV contrast: to evaluate for the cause of a suspected <u>CSF leak</u>

* CT or <u>MR angiography</u> and <u>venography</u>: to evaluate for <u>blunt cerebrovascular injury</u>

* Ophthalmic <u>ultrasound</u>: can help detect <u>ocular injuries</u> (e.g., <u>vitreous hemorrhage</u>, <u>retinal detachment</u>, globe rupture)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Basilar skull fractures</u> can injure the <u>internal carotid artery</u>. Obtain urgent <u>CT angiography</u> head in patients with signs of <u>carotid-cavernous fistula</u> or <u>stroke</u>. [[4]](/library/CNbqW8)




![Anterior skull base fractures](media/h5rpdp8xdyfe9ffhlh6ncc0w.jpg)

Anterior skull base fractures




### Management [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[8]](/library/U0cb2a0)




#### Initial management




* Initiate <u>immediate management of skull fractures</u>.

* Consider <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for skull fractures</u> for patients with persistent <u>CSF</u> leakage (> 7 days).  [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[9]](/library/v0bA3H)





#### Definitive management




* <u>Conservative management</u>

* Mainstay for most <u>basilar skull fractures</u> without severe intracranial neurovascular complications

* May include <u>CSF leak precautions</u> and/or <u>corticosteroids</u> for incomplete <u>traumatic facial nerve palsy</u>

* Surgical management

* Emergency <u>surgery</u> may be indicated for comminuted or displaced <u>fractures</u>, large <u>CSF leaks</u>, or significant neurovascular complications

* Delayed repair of persistent (longer than 3–7 days) small-moderate <u>CSF leaks</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid nasogastric tubes and <u>nasotracheal intubation</u> in patients with a suspected <u>ethmoid bone</u> <u>fracture</u>, as they may cause direct intracranial injury.




#### Disposition




* Consult neurosurgery.

* Admit all patients for observation.





### Complications




#### Liquorrhea




* Definition: external leakage of <u>CSF</u> via a dural tear [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* CSF rhinorrhea: leakage of <u>CSF</u> from the nose

* CSF otorrhea: leakage of <u>CSF</u> from the <u>external auditory meatus</u>

* Pathophysiology: dural tear (most often due to <u>basilar skull fractures</u>) → communication between the <u>subarachnoid space</u> and <u>middle ear</u> and/or <u>paranasal sinuses</u> → <u>CSF leak</u> [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Etiology [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/nG17-R0)

* Craniofacial trauma (e.g., <u>basilar skull fractures</u>)

* <u>Iatrogenic</u> trauma

* <u>Neoplasia</u>

* Clinical features [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/nG17-R0)

* Intermittent clear or blood-tinged watery discharge from the nose and/or <u>ear</u>

* Worsens with dependent head positioning

* Sweet or salty <u>post-nasal drip</u>

* Symptoms resembling <u>post-lumbar puncture headache</u> can occur.

* <u>Meningismus</u> may develop.

* Diagnostics [[5]](/library/KnbU88)[[10]](/library/nG17-R0)

* CSF detection studies

* <u>Halo sign</u> (bedside study): rapidly expanding ring of clear fluid surrounding blood; produced after a drop of discharge is applied to gauze or tissue paper  [[11]](/library/e0cxUa0)

* Detection of β2-transferrin (<u>gold standard</u>): an isoform of <u>transferrin</u> found primarily in <u>CSF</u> and <u>perilymph</u>  [[5]](/library/KnbU88)[[10]](/library/nG17-R0)

* Imaging: localization of dural tears with <u>high-resolution CT</u>, <u>MRI</u>, and/or <u>nasal endoscopy</u>

* Treatment [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[8]](/library/U0cb2a0)[[10]](/library/nG17-R0)

* Consult neurosurgery.

* CSF leak precautions

* Bed rest with the head of the bed elevated to ≥ 30°

* Avoidance of straining and <u>Valsalva maneuver</u> (e.g., sneezing, nose blowing, <u>incentive spirometry</u>)

* Use of <u>stool softeners</u> to prevent straining with defecation

* Consider <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for skull fractures</u> for patients with persistent <u>CSF</u> leakage (> 7 days).  [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[9]](/library/v0bA3H)

* Nonsurgical management: usually sufficient for small-moderate traumatic <u>CSF leaks</u>, as most resolve without complications within 1 week

* Surgical management

* Consider for large leaks or persistent (longer than 3–7 days) small-moderate leaks

* May involve transcranial or endoscopic repair and/or <u>CSF</u> diversion with external <u>ventriculostomy</u> or lumbar drain





#### Other complications




* <u>Meningitis</u>

* <u>Pneumocephalus</u>

* <u>Panhypopituitarism</u>

* See also “Complications” in “<u>Temporal bones</u> <u>fractures</u>.”

## Temporal bone fractures

### Definition




* <u>Fracture</u> of the <u>temporal bone</u>, typically involving the petrous portion

* Often associated with <u>epidural hematoma</u> due to proximity of the <u>temporal bone</u> to the <u>middle meningeal artery</u>





### Etiology




* High-energy <u>blunt trauma</u> to the <u>temporal bone</u> (often in association with <u>polytrauma</u>)

* Most common cause: traffic-related injuries (e.g., <u>motor vehicle collisions</u>, bicycle vs. pedestrian collisions)





### Clinical features




* Injury to the <u>external auditory canal</u> and <u>tympanic membrane</u> is common.

* <u>Cranial nerve palsies</u> (<u>CN I</u>, <u>CN V</u>, <u>CN VI</u>, <u>CN VII</u>, <u>CN VIII</u>)

* Injury to the <u>otic capsule</u> significantly increases the risk of <u>facial nerve palsy</u>, <u>CSF leak</u>, and <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>.

* <u>Signs of TBI</u> may be present.





| <br>Clinical features of petrous bone fractures by classification [[12]](/library/S0cy2a0)[[13]](/library/bH1HKR0)[[14]](/library/YH1nKR0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Longitudinal <u>fracture</u> | Transverse <u>fracture</u> |
| Impact | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> or temporal force<br><br> | <br>* Frontal or occipital force<br><br> |
| Clinical features | <br><br>* Damage to the <u>middle ear</u><br><br>* <u>Ruptured tympanic membrane</u><br><br>* <u>Otorrhagia</u><br><br>* <u>Conductive hearing loss</u> (due to <u>dislocation</u> of the <u>auditory ossicles</u>)<br><br>* Possibly <u>CSF otorrhea</u> in the event of dural <u>laceration</u><br><br>* <u>Peripheral facial nerve paralysis</u>  [[12]](/library/S0cy2a0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Damage to the <u>inner ear</u><br><br>* <u>Hemotympanum</u><br><br>* <u>Sensorineural hearing loss</u><br><br>* <u>Vertigo</u>, <u>nausea</u>, and <u>spontaneous nystagmus</u><br><br>* Peripheral facial <u>paralysis</u><br><br><br> |
| Otoscopic findings | <br>* <u>Ruptured eardrum</u><br><br> | <br>* Intact <u>eardrum</u><br><br> |





![Longitudinal and transverse temporal bone fractures](media/rwkdjwk9d7gj9l0x42zk93lq.jpg)

Longitudinal and transverse temporal bone fractures

![Hemotympanum](media/qvhad3vdvrd94hyykbgd0a4u.jpg)

Hemotympanum




### Diagnostics [[12]](/library/S0cy2a0)[[13]](/library/bH1HKR0)




See also “Diagnostics” in “<u>Basilar skull fractures</u>.”




* Imaging

* CT head without IV contrast (preferred modality): usually sufficient to diagnose <u>temporal bone fractures</u>

* <u>Fracture</u> lines in the petrous part of the <u>temporal bone</u>

* <u>Hyperdensity</u> in the <u>mastoid air cells</u>: indicates hemorrhage

* <u>High-resolution CT</u> of the <u>temporal bone</u>: to evaluate <u>facial nerve paralysis</u>, <u>CSF</u> leakage, or a suspected vascular injury

* <u>Otoscopy</u>: to inspect the <u>tympanic membrane</u> (see “<u>Clinical features of petrous bone fractures</u>”)

* <u>CSF detection studies</u>: to assess for <u>CSF</u> leakage in <u>otorrhea</u>





### Treatment [[13]](/library/bH1HKR0)




* <u>Surgery</u> may be indicated for: [[12]](/library/S0cy2a0)

* Dural repair

* <u>Middle ear</u> reconstruction

* <u>Facial nerve</u> decompression or grafting

* See also “Treatment” in “<u>Basilar skull fracture</u>” and “<u>Management of traumatic facial nerve palsy</u>.”





### Complications




#### Perilymphatic fistula [[15]](/library/a1WQ240)




* Definition: : an abnormal connection between the perilymphatic space in the <u>inner ear</u> and the <u>middle ear</u>, mastoid, or intracranial cavity, resulting in <u>perilymph</u> leakage

* Etiology

* Trauma: <u>temporal bone fractures</u>, <u>barotrauma</u> (e.g., <u>Valsalva maneuver</u>), penetrating <u>ear trauma</u>, <u>ear</u> <u>surgery</u> (e.g., <u>stapedectomy</u>)

* Congenital <u>temporal bone</u> abnormalities

* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* Clinical features

* Acute onset of <u>vertigo</u>, disequilibrium, <u>tinnitus</u>, <u>sensorineural hearing loss</u>, and/or <u>aural fullness</u>

* Vestibular symptoms typically worsen with loud noises (Tullio phenomenon) and pressure changes in the <u>middle ear</u> or <u>external auditory canal</u> (Hennebert sign)

* Diagnostics: <u>CT scan</u>, <u>MRI</u> scan

* Treatment: surgical <u>fistula</u> closure





#### Other complications




* <u>Traumatic facial nerve palsy</u>

* Posttraumatic <u>benign paroxysmal positional vertigo</u>

* Traumatic <u>endolymphatic hydrops</u>

* See also “Complications” in “<u>Basilar skull fractures</u>.”





![Course and branches of the facial nerve (VII)](media/lw99heghm7w3d7zwzouhqm5m.jpg)
